**Title:** Which Dollar Broke? Separating Token Failures from Platform-Ledger Failures in Web Dollar Markets

**Abstract (286 words):**

Crypto prices on the Web are quoted in two kinds of dollar: stablecoin tokens, and balances in an exchange's internal ledger that reach the banking system only through the platform's rails. When a dollar price moves away from par, users, price feeds and oracles need to know which of the two failed, and we know of no measure that separates them. This is hard because a ledger's value is never quoted directly, public prices are asynchronous last trades that thin out under stress, and any single asset may carry its own shock. We price the platform's dollar through an unpegged asset (BTC) against a venue whose rails stay open, which splits a dollar-quoted dislocation into a token and a ledger component. We accept the split only when unrelated assets agree and the venue's internal cross-rates hold. On Binance.US, the method attributes all but 6% of the USDC dislocation in the March 2023 bank run to the token. After the exchange's banks withdrew in June 2023, it attributes 99% of the dislocation to the platform's dollar, which traded at a discount while withdrawals were threatened and at a premium of several percent once only withdrawals remained open. The pattern holds in three assets, against a second reference and in an active market, and the gap closed when the rails returned. Run hourly over 10 months, the method flags ledger failure in 67.7% of rail-cut hours (in sample; 56 to 76% across 9 threshold settings), in 1.1% of calm hours, and in no SVB or FTX hour under any setting. Sterling and euro rail cuts show only small effects. All findings are descriptive: the token-side multi-event study was pre-registered, and the ledger analysis came from a disclosed search.

**Suggested keywords:** stablecoins; platform money; exchange ledgers; price feeds and oracles; Web measurement; natural experiment; reproducibility
